stem: A Massachusetts collaborating pharmacist orders a laboratory test directly related to the drug therapy she co-manages, under an approved protocol for her setting and in direct consultation with the supervising physician, and then evaluates the result. Her evaluation concludes that the patient has a new condition. What is the position?

choices.text: The ordering may be proper, but the evaluation may not include a diagnostic component.
The ordering is improper, because a pharmacist may not order laboratory tests.
Both are proper, because the test was directly related to the therapy managed.
Both are improper, because laboratory work sits outside collaborative management.
Both are proper, provided she reports the conclusion to the supervising physician.

explanation.core_reasoning: The laboratory limb of the statutory collaborative-management definition permits ordering and evaluating results directly related to drug therapy under physician supervision or direct consultation and an approved protocol, but only WHEN THE EVALUATION SHALL NOT INCLUDE A DIAGNOSTIC COMPONENT. Satisfying the conditions for ordering does not enlarge what the evaluation may conclude.

choice_analysis.A: Correct: the conditions on ordering and the limit on evaluating are separate.
choice_analysis.B: Ordering is permitted on the stated conditions, which were met here.
choice_analysis.C: Relatedness to the therapy does not lift the diagnostic limit.
choice_analysis.D: Laboratory work is expressly within the definition on conditions.
choice_analysis.E: Reporting the conclusion does not cure a diagnostic evaluation.

related_facts: The same definition also permits collecting histories and checking vital signs
explanation.mpje_trap: Candidates treat compliance with the ordering conditions as authorising whatever the evaluation then finds.

reasoning_steps: Check the conditions attached to ordering the test
Check the separate limit attached to evaluating the result
Conclude that the second limit is unaffected by satisfying the first
